e.etymology: A blend of English Athena and Spanish Atenea, both names of the Greek goddess of wisdom and war, patron of Athens. The meaning of her name is unknown.
A spelling of Vedant, from Sanskrit Vedanta, the end of the Vedas: the Upanishads and the school of Hindu philosophy built on them.
Hebrew yafa means beautiful. Yafa is also the Arabic name of the port city of Jaffa, and Palestinian families give it in the city's honor.
The name of a champion in the video game League of Legends, the Blade Dancer of Ionia. Its makers at Riot Games have given it no meaning.

assoc.t: Irelia, a champion in the game League of Legends

e.etymology: A variant of Gary, a medieval short form of Germanic names beginning with ger or gar, spear, such as Gerald and Gerard. Gary took off after actor Gary Cooper.
namesakes: Garry Shandling (comedian, The Larry Sanders Show)
Garry Marshall (creator of Happy Days, director of Pretty Woman)

e.etymology: A pet form of Timothy, from Greek Timotheos: time, honor, plus theos, god.
namesakes: Timmy Turner (hero of The Fairly OddParents)
Timmy Martin (the boy on the TV series Lassie)

e.etymology: From Latin nona, ninth, the feminine of the Roman name Nonus. English-speaking families once gave it to a ninth child.
e.note: Sounds like nonna, the Italian word for grandmother.

e.etymology: A spelling of Lindsey or Lindsay, a Scottish surname from Lindsey in Lincolnshire, Old English for the island of Lind, the old name of Lincoln.
The Dutch and Low German short form of Diederik, their form of Theodoric, from Germanic words for people and ruler. Derek is the English counterpart.
namesakes: Dirk Nowitzki (Dallas Mavericks Hall of Famer)
Dirk Diggler (lead character of Boogie Nights)
e.note: A dirk is also a Scottish dagger.

e.etymology: Entered American use in 1974 with the TV drama Nakia, about a Navajo deputy. It is sometimes linked to an Arabic word for pure and drew new notice from Nakia in Marvel's Black Panther.
namesakes: Nakia (Wakandan spy played by Lupita Nyong'o in Black Panther)

assoc.t: Nakia, Wakandan spy in Marvel's Black Panther

e.etymology: A pet form of Vincent, from Latin vincens, conquering. In the 1800s it was also a girls' name, short for Lavinia.
namesakes: Vinnie Barbarino (John Travolta's character on Welcome Back, Kotter)

e.etymology: An American name of the 1990s, a spelling of Kiana or Ke- plus Anna, that rose alongside Kiana and Keanu.
A short form of Randall and Randolph, whose first part is the Germanic word rand, the rim of a shield.
namesakes: Rand al'Thor (hero of The Wheel of Time)

assoc.t: Ayn Rand, author of Atlas Shrugged
Rand al'Thor, hero of The Wheel of Time

e.etymology: In the US a variant of Jalen and Jaylon, modern names built on Ja- and -len. A Jalon also appears once in the Bible, in a genealogy in 1 Chronicles.
An English surname used as a first name, as in the middle name of suffragist Elizabeth Cady Stanton, and a variant of Kady. Cady Heron is the lead in the film Mean Girls.
namesakes: Cady Heron (Lindsay Lohan's character in Mean Girls)

assoc.t: Cady Heron, heroine of Mean Girls

e.etymology: An English surname, and the ordinary word shade, used as a boys' name in the 19th-century United States and again recently.
e.note: Throwing shade is slang for a subtle insult, so expect some jokes.

assoc.t: shade, shelter from the sun; throwing shade, a sly insult

e.etymology: An American blend of the De- prefix and Marius, a Roman family name. It sits close to Demarcus and Damarius.
A modern American name that rhymes with Gavin and sits near Tavian and Tevin.
A spelling of Casey, an Irish surname from Ó Cathasaigh, descendant of Cathasach, a byname meaning vigilant. Cayce is also a surname in its own right, as in the psychic Edgar Cayce.
A new American spelling of Aidan, from Irish Aodhán, a pet form of Aodh, fire, and the name of a 7th-century Irish saint.
A Latinate form of Katherine, from Greek Aikaterine. The original meaning is debated; Christians long tied it to katharos, pure. Shakespeare used it for the heroine of The Taming of the Shrew.
namesakes: Katherina Minola (the shrew in Shakespeare's The Taming of the Shrew)

e.etymology: A variant of Callie, a pet form of Caroline and of Greek names beginning with Calli-, from kallos, beauty.
e.note: The single L leads some readers to say KAY-lee.

e.etymology: From Arabic Lamya, in classical usage a woman with dark, beautiful lips, and widely explained today as shining or radiant.
e.note: In Greek myth Lamia is a child-devouring monster, and lamia is an old English word for a female demon.

e.etymology: An alternative spelling of Adeline, from Old French Adeline, a diminutive of Adela and Adele, built on the Germanic word adal, noble. The Normans brought it to England.
A respelling of Fallon, an Irish surname from Ó Fallamháin, descendant of Fallamhán, a name meaning leader. Fallon Carrington of the TV series Dynasty made it a girls' name.
A spelling of Shirley, an English place name and surname from Old English scir, bright, and leah, clearing. This spelling is common in Latin America and Indonesia.
A spelling of Eloise shaped by Ella and Louise. Eloise is from French Héloïse, probably the Germanic name Helewidis, built on words for healthy and wide.
An American blend of the Ja- prefix with Gabriel. It is also close to Jibril, the Arabic form of the archangel's name.
An American blend of the Ja- prefix and Kyla.
